questions.topic: Water heating energy and a heat pump
questions.learningObjective: State the coefficient of performance from a measured heat and electricity pair
questions.stem: The honey room uses a small heat pump water heater that delivered 55.2 kWh of heat in February while drawing 18.4 kWh of electricity. Which statement describes that month correctly?

options.text: The unit ran at a coefficient of performance of 0.33, because 18.4 over 55.2 is the ratio.
options.misconception: inverts heat delivered and electricity used

options.text: The unit ran at a coefficient of performance of 3.0.
The unit ran at a coefficient of performance of 36.8, because 55.2 plus 18.4 is the energy moved.
options.misconception: adds heat and electricity instead of dividing them

options.text: The unit ran at a coefficient of performance of 1.0.
options.misconception: treats a heat pump like a resistance heater

questions.explanation: The coefficient of performance is heat delivered over electricity consumed, so 55.2 over 18.4 is exactly 3.0. The machine moves heat rather than generating it, so output can exceed input.
questions.hint: Divide heat delivered by electricity consumed.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a fleet capacity factor is derived from energy and ratings
questions.stem: Five electric fence energisers serve the apiary and the log records a combined rated output of 1.2 kW, 1,570 hours of operation across the season and 1,410 kWh delivered in total. Explain how a fleet capacity factor is worked out from those numbers and what it tells you.

answer.exemplar: A fleet capacity factor compares the energy the units actually produced with the energy they could have produced at rated power over the hours they were available. With a combined rating of 1.2 kW over 1,570 hours the maximum is 1,884 kWh, so the fleet factor is 1,410 over 1,884, about 0.75. That says the fences ran near three quarters of their possible output for the hours they were in use.

questions.explanation: The fleet factor uses combined rated power and the hours available, so 1.2 kW over 1,570 hours gives a maximum of 1,884 kWh. Delivered 1,410 over that is about 0.75.
questions.hint: Multiply the combined rating by the hours available.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a heat recovery saving and its annual extrapolation

stimulus.body: Honey room extraction notes: the extractor was running with the extraction fan at full speed and the door closed for 45 minutes each week. A trial was then run with a heat recovery unit on the extract and the fan on minimum, recording 6.1 kWh for the same 45 minute slot against 9.4 kWh before.

questions.stem: The extraction notes below give two slots of the same fan. What saving does the heat recovery unit deliver on the extraction slot, and what limits how far that saving can be carried across the year?

options.text: About 3.3 kWh each session, or 172 kWh a year if the weekly slot continues through the season.
options.misconception: extrapolates a weekly trial straight.

options.text: About 6.1 kWh each session, since that is the energy the unit now uses instead of the old figure.
options.misconception: reports the new consumption as if it were the saving

options.text: About 3.3 kWh each session, which is 35 percent of the old figure.
About 12.7 kWh each session, because the recovery unit adds its own fan energy on top of the original draw.
options.misconception: adds the recovery fan's own energy to the saving

questions.explanation: The saving is 9.4 minus 6.1, which is 3.3 kWh per session, about 35 percent of the old draw. That covers the 45 minute extraction slot only, since the fan is off the rest of the day.
questions.hint: Subtract the two readings, then check what hours they cover.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a measurement of desalination specific energy use
questions.stem: The apiary needs brackish water for washing and I am considering a small reverse osmosis unit. Describe how I would measure its monthly energy use and the consumption figure I would report.

answer.exemplar: Record the incoming and outgoing water volumes from the unit's own meters over a full month of typical washing, together with the electricity metered at the unit's supply. Compute the specific energy consumption by dividing the metered electricity in kWh by the permeate volume in cubic metres, and report it in kWh per cubic metre alongside the feed and brine volumes and the salt content of the feed water. Repeat over a second month, since a single month can be distorted by heavy washing days.

questions.explanation: A meaningful figure needs the electricity metered at the unit and the water produced in the same period, so the two can be divided. The period must be representative.
questions.hint: Divide metered electricity by permeate volume.

questions.learningObjective: Compute specific electricity use and hydrogen yield for electrolysis
questions.stem: The log for the apiary trailer records that 14.0 kWh of electricity from the roof array went into an electrolyser that produced 0.32 kg of hydrogen. What specific electricity use does that represent, and how much hydrogen could be made from 250 kWh of electricity?

options.text: About 0.023 kWh per kilogram, so 250 kWh would produce more than ten kilograms of hydrogen.
options.misconception: inverts the ratio and scales the error into the mass

options.text: About 28 kWh per kilogram, because half the electricity was used for compression and purification.
options.misconception: invents an unlogged loss and changes the measured figure

options.text: About 43.75 kWh per kilogram, so 250 kWh would produce roughly 5.7 kg of hydrogen at that rate.
About 43.75 kWh per kilogram, but 250 kWh would produce only about 3.2 kg of hydrogen.
options.misconception: applies the hydrogen mass instead of the energy per kilogram

questions.explanation: Specific use is electricity over hydrogen produced, so 14.0 kWh per 0.32 kg is 43.75 kWh per kilogram. At that rate 250 kWh gives 250 over 43.75, about 5.7 kg.
questions.hint: Divide electricity by the hydrogen mass, then scale up.

questions.learningObjective: Correct an unweighted average of monthly coefficients of performance
questions.stem: The honey room heat pump gave a coefficient of performance of 2.4 in December, 3.1 in January and 1.6 in February, and the manager reported an average of 2.37 for the winter. What is wrong with that average, and what should it be?

options.text: Nothing is wrong, because a simple mean of monthly coefficients is the standard seasonal figure.
options.misconception: believes an unweighted mean of ratios is correct

options.text: The average must be weighted by energy, so 116 kWh over 50.9 kWh gives about 2.28 rather than 2.37.
The figure is wrong because monthly coefficients should be averaged as percentages and converted back after.
options.misconception: invents a percentage conversion that changes nothing

options.misconception: cherry-picks the best months for the average

questions.explanation: A seasonal coefficient is total heat over total electricity, so 116 kWh over 50.9 kWh gives about 2.28. The simple mean of the three monthly ratios is 2.37.
questions.hint: Weight each month by the energy it actually used.

questions.stem: Why is heating degree days a useful normalising measure when comparing gas use across the apiary's sheds?

options.text: Because it adjusts gas use for how cold it was, so sheds can be compared fairly across months.
Because it converts gas use into a number that can be compared directly with electricity use.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain how heat recovery changes the energy balance of extraction
questions.stem: The honey room loses a lot of warm air because the extractor runs during every session. Explain how a heat recovery unit changes the energy picture and what has to be measured to judge the benefit.

answer.exemplar: The extractor carries warm, moisture-laden room air out of the building and drags in cold outdoor air, so the fan energy and the heating of that replacement air are both part of the cost. A heat recovery unit transfers heat from the outgoing air to the incoming air, so the supply air arrives warmer and the boiler has less to do. To judge the benefit you must record the electricity used by the fans and the heating energy saved for the same hours, which needs a temporary temperature and flow measurement rather than an estimate.

questions.explanation: Heat recovery lowers the energy needed to warm the incoming air by transferring warmth from the outgoing stream, so it cuts heating demand rather than fan power.
questions.hint: Two separate loads change, and both must be measured.

questions.learningObjective: Compute specific energy use of a reverse osmosis unit from a diagram
questions.stem: A diagram for the apiary's brackish water unit shows raw water at 8 litres per minute into a pre-filter, then a reverse osmosis membrane producing 5.2 litres per minute of permeate with the rest leaving as brine, then a 400 W booster pump and a 900 W high pressure pump. What is the electricity use per cubic metre of permeate?

options.text: About 4.17 kWh per cubic metre, from 1.3 kW against 0.312 cubic metres of permeate each hour.
About 0.25 kWh per cubic metre, because 0.4 plus 0.9 kilowatts is the energy for each cubic metre.
options.misconception: treats the pump power as an energy per unit volume

options.text: About 3.68 kWh per cubic metre, because the brine stream means only 5.2 litres a minute count as product.
options.misconception: double counts the brine when adjusting the permeate rate

options.text: About 8.33 kWh per cubic metre, because the raw flow of 8 litres per minute should be used as the product.
options.misconception: uses the raw feed volume instead of the permeate volume

questions.explanation: The two pumps draw 1.3 kW and produce 0.312 cubic metres of permeate each hour, so specific energy is 1.3 over 0.312, about 4.17 kWh per cubic metre. The brine leaves rather than being delivered.
questions.hint: Product volume per hour divided into pump energy per hour.

questions.learningObjective: Split electrolysis and compression energy in a hydrogen trial

stimulus.body: Electrolyser trial at the apiary workshop: array delivered 4.1 kWh on a sunny afternoon; the unit ran for 1.6 hours at 2.1 kW; 0.048 kg of hydrogen was collected and compressed to 30 bar using a compressor drawing 180 W.

options.text: About 85 kWh per kilogram, because every kWh the array produced must be charged to the hydrogen.

About 13.1 kWh per kilogram, because 4.1 kWh from the array was shared with the afternoon's other uses.

questions.explanation: The electrolyser used 3.36 kWh and the compressor 0.29 kWh, so 3.65 kWh produced 0.048 kg, about 76 kWh per kilogram with compression near 8 percent.

questions.stem: I want a fair seasonal figure for the heat pump that heats the honey room. Describe the measurement method and how you would report the result.

answer.exemplar: Meter the heat pump's electricity consumption and the heat delivered to the store, reading both at the same intervals through the whole season, and keep the storage temperature and the room temperature alongside so heat held in the tank can be separated from heat actually used. Calculate the seasonal coefficient of performance as total heat delivered over total electricity used, and report it with the mean monthly value and the coldest month value, because a single mean hides how the machine performs at low temperatures.

questions.explanation: A seasonal figure needs metered electricity and metered heat over the same period, with heat left in storage separated from heat actually used. A mean alone hides performance in the coldest weeks.
questions.hint: Separate stored heat from heat actually used.

questions.stem: Why is a heat pump generally the better choice than a resistance element for heating the honey room store?

options.text: Because a heat pump heats faster, so the store reaches temperature in less time.
options.misconception: confuses heating speed with energy efficiency

options.text: Because it moves existing heat rather than generating it.
Because a heat pump needs no maintenance and lasts longer than any resistance element.
options.misconception: assumes maintenance-free operation and long life

options.text: Because the heat pump can also cool the store in summer at no extra cost.
options.misconception: assumes cooling comes free once the unit is installed

questions.explanation: A resistance element turns every unit of electricity into one unit of heat, while a heat pump transfers heat and can deliver several units of heat per unit of electricity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Separate the two energy effects of a heat recovery unit
questions.stem: The honey room extractor runs 4.5 hours a week through the season, and a heat recovery unit on the extract would let the fan run at a lower speed. Explain the two separate energy effects involved and how they should be measured.

answer.exemplar: Two effects must be separated. First, the recovery unit pre-heats the incoming air, so the boiler has less to supply during those hours; this shows up as reduced gas or heating energy in the same week. Second, the fan can run at a reduced speed because the resistance of the duct has fallen, which may cut the fan's own electricity. Measuring only the fan meter would show the second effect and hide the first, so the heating fuel and the fan electricity should both be logged for the same hours before and after the change.

questions.explanation: Heat recovery changes the heating energy needed and may also change the fan electricity, and only the second appears on the fan meter. The heating saving is the larger effect.
questions.hint: One effect is on the heating, one on the fan.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why hydrogen routes lose energy over a full cycle
questions.stem: Making hydrogen with an electrolyser costs far more electricity than the hydrogen later delivers when burned or used in a fuel cell. Explain why the two numbers differ and what that implies for using the apiary's spare solar output.

answer.exemplar: Electrolysis stores energy in chemical bonds with losses at every stage, so a kilogram of hydrogen typically needs somewhere around 50 kWh of electricity to produce, and compression and storage add more. A fuel cell releases about half of that energy as electricity, so the round trip from solar panel to wheel is roughly a third or less of the original generation. For an apiary with occasional surplus solar output, the electricity is therefore better used directly on site, unless the hydrogen is needed for seasonal storage or for a vehicle that cannot use the array.

questions.explanation: Electrolysis and later fuel cell use each carry losses, so the round trip from array to useful power is well below one hundred percent. Hydrogen therefore consumes more electricity than it returns.
questions.hint: Each conversion step in the chain loses energy.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a combined coefficient for several appliances
questions.stem: Several appliances in the honey room have published coefficients of performance, and I want one combined figure for the room. Describe how you would produce that number and what you would need to be careful about.

answer.exemplar: Collect the electricity consumed and the useful heat delivered by each appliance over the same period, using submeters rather than estimates, and combine them as total heat over total electricity. A single figure built from an average of separate coefficients will be wrong unless every appliance contributed equally, which is rarely true, and the period must cover a full cycle of use so a month does not miss one duty.

questions.explanation: A combined figure must add the useful output and input of each appliance before dividing, because they contribute unequally and run for different hours.
questions.hint: Add the heats and the electricity first, then divide.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a monthly desalination energy figure covers
questions.stem: The apiary's brackish water unit uses 58.8 kWh a month to make 12.0 cubic metres of permeate, and the feed water has 1,800 milligrams per litre of salt. Explain what the monthly energy figure covers and why the salt content matters to the running cost.

answer.exemplar: The 58.8 kWh covers the electricity used by the unit and its auxiliaries while producing 12.0 cubic metres of permeate, so it is a whole-plant operating figure rather than the cost of the membranes alone. Feed salinity sets the osmotic pressure that the pump must overcome, so a higher salt content means a higher pressure and more energy for the same volume of water. Doubling the salt content will therefore raise the monthly energy use even though nothing else has changed.

questions.explanation: The monthly figure is a whole-plant operating number covering pumps, controls and pretreatment for the water produced. Feed salinity raises the osmotic pressure to be overcome, so more power is drawn.
questions.hint: Higher salt means the pump must push harder.

answer.exemplar: Measure the hot water volume and temperature actually drawn in a typical week, including any washing and the hive warming, and add the standing heat losses of the store for the same hours. questions.explanation: Sizing needs the hot water actually drawn and the heat lost from the store over the same period, so the unit matches a real duty cycle. Choosing by floor area ignores that duty.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why extraction ventilation dominates the energy cost
questions.stem: The extract fan in the honey room runs at 1,450 W and pulls warm air out of the building every session. Explain, in terms of energy, why this matters and what a heat recovery unit does about it.

answer.exemplar: The fan itself uses a small amount of electricity, but it removes warm air from the building, and the heating system then has to supply heat for every cubic metre of cold outdoor air that comes in to replace it. Over a season that replacement heating is normally far larger than the fan electricity. A heat recovery unit transfers heat from the outgoing air to the incoming air, so the incoming air arrives warmer and the boiler has less work to do, while the fan may also run more slowly.

questions.explanation: The fan's own electricity is small next to the heating energy needed to warm the replacement air, so ventilation dominates the cost of extraction.
questions.hint: The fan power is not the main cost.

options.text: About 50 percent, because the room air is four degrees warmer than the supply air it receives.
options.misconception: compares the wrong pair of temperatures

questions.explanation: Recovery efficiency is the supply air rise over the extract to outdoor difference, so 8 over 12 is about 67 percent. Some energy is lost in passing the air, so the transfer is never complete.
questions.hint: Compare the supply rise with the full available difference.

questions.learningObjective: Read specific consumption and recovery from a monthly record

stimulus.body: Monthly figures for the apiary's water unit: permeate delivered 12.0 cubic metres, brine leaving 2.6 cubic metres, feed water taken 14.6 cubic metres, electricity at the unit's supply 58.8 kWh, feed salinity 1,800 milligrams per litre. The same month the plant was run only for the two washing days.

questions.stem: The monthly figures for the apiary's water unit are set out below. What does the record show about specific energy consumption and about how much of the feed water becomes usable product?

options.text: About 4.9 kWh per cubic metre and about 82 percent recovery, so the brine stream is fairly small.
options.misconception: calls the brine small without noticing it is not product

options.text: About 2.0 kWh per cubic metre and about 82 percent recovery.
options.misconception: uses the brine volume as the useful product

options.text: About 4.9 kWh per cubic metre and about 82 percent recovery, so most of the feed water becomes usable product.
About 5.4 kWh per cubic metre and about 76 percent recovery.
options.misconception: uses the feed volume as the product in both calculations

questions.explanation: Specific consumption is 58.8 over 12.0 cubic metres, which is 4.9 kWh per cubic metre, and recovery is 12.0 over 14.6, about 82 percent. The brine leaves the system.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of a fleet against a single array
questions.stem: I want to know how well the apiary's array fleet is performing compared with a single larger array. Describe the measurement method and the comparison you would make.

answer.exemplar: Record the electricity delivered by each array over a full year and note the rated capacity of each, then compute a capacity factor for each unit as its delivered energy over its rating multiplied by the hours in the year. Repeat for the fleet as a whole by adding the delivered energy and the ratings before dividing. Compare the fleet figure with the best single unit and with the worst, and check whether any difference comes from outages, shading or soiling rather than from the equipment itself.

questions.explanation: Each unit needs its own delivered energy and rating over the same hours, and the fleet figure is a ratio of totals rather than an average of members.
questions.hint: Compute a factor per unit, then a factor for the totals.

options.text: Route B, by about 0.33 kg per 100 kWh, because its lower electrolysis energy is not cancelled by compression.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Compute a combined coefficient of performance for two machines
questions.stem: One heat pump delivers 120 kWh of heat using 60 kWh of electricity, and another delivers 120 kWh of heat using 40 kWh of electricity. What is the combined coefficient of performance of the two machines working together?
questions.explanation: The combined coefficient is total heat over total electricity, so 240 kWh over 100 kWh is 2.4. Averaging the two machine values would give 2.5, because a simple mean weights them equally.
questions.hint: Add the heats and the electricity, then divide.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why operating hours matter to a lighting saving
questions.stem: Why should a lighting retrofit be judged against the hours the lights are actually on rather than against the old lamp's wattage alone?

options.text: Because the wattage of the old lamp says nothing about how many hours the room needs light.
options.misconception: denies that the old wattage is useful evidence

options.text: Because the saving depends on hours of use as well as power, so a lower wattage can still waste energy.
Because lighting hours are the only factor that matters and the power of the lamp can be ignored.
options.misconception: overstates the case for operating hours

options.text: Because retrofit savings should always be reported in kilowatt hours per month rather than per lamp.
options.misconception: prescribes a reporting unit without a physical reason

questions.explanation: A lighting saving is the difference in power multiplied by the hours of use, so both must be known. Lowering the wattage while extending the hours can leave the energy use unchanged.
questions.hint: Energy is power multiplied by time.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Water heating energy and a heat pump
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a higher coefficient on cost and sizing
questions.stem: A coefficient of performance of 2.5 means the honey room heat pump delivers 2.5 units of heat for each unit of electricity, while the resistance element it replaced delivers exactly one. Explain what that difference means for the electricity bill and for the size of any future unit.

answer.exemplar: At a coefficient of performance of 2.5 the heat pump draws 0.4 kWh of electricity for every 1 kWh of hot water, where the element draws 1 kWh, so the same hot water costs two and a half times less in electricity from the pump alone. A future replacement should be sized on the heat actually required rather than on the pump's electrical rating, because the electrical input is a fraction of the heat delivered. The difference also means the electrical supply and cabling need less capacity than for a resistance element of the same output.

questions.explanation: A higher coefficient of performance means less electricity for the same heat, so the electricity used falls in proportion to the ratio. It also changes how a replacement is sized.
questions.hint: The output is bigger than the electrical input.
